front.title: Framework and YANG Data Model for the NMA A2U Interface

author.organization: China Academy of Information and Communication Technology

abstract.t: This document describes a framework and a YANG data model for the Agent-to-User (A2U) interface of a Network Management Agent (NMA). The A2U interface is a user-facing interface through which a non-agent upper-layer system or user, such as an operator's OSS/BSS, orchestrator, management portal, human-facing application, automation system, etc., interacts with an NMA.

The A2U interface supports NMA capability discovery, unified intent submission, task lifecycle management, execution plan exposure, human-in-the-loop confirmation, event notification, and consistent error reporting.

The YANG data model defined in this document describes protocol-binding-independent information objects and message structures used by the A2U interface. This document does not mandate a specific protocol binding. An HTTP-based realization using JSON and Server-Sent Events (SSE) is provided as a non-normative example.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Telecommunication networks are becoming increasingly complex in scale, technology composition, service diversity, and operational requirements. Traditional manual operation and fixed API-based management are often insufficient to support highly automated and adaptive network operations.

A Network Management Agent (NMA) is an autonomous or semi-autonomous management entity with awareness, analysis, decision-making, and execution capabilities. It can interpret user goals, plan management actions, invoke tools and interfaces, monitor execution, and report results.
To allow non-agent upper-layer systems and users to consume NMA capabilities in a uniform way, this document defines the Agent-to-User (A2U) interface.
The A2U interface supports:

A2U is intended for client/server-style interaction between a non-agent upper-layer system or user and an NMA. It is not intended for communication between an upper-layer NMA and a lower-layer NMA. NMA-to-NMA or Agent-to-Agent communication is outside the scope of A2U and is expected to use A2A or other Agent-to-Agent interfaces.

The A2U YANG data model is protocol-binding independent. It describes the information exchanged across the A2U interface, but it does not require that A2U objects be exposed as configuration datastore nodes.

An HTTP-based realization is provided in Appendix A. In such a realization, A2U may use /nma/a2u/* resources and be logically separated from the traditional RESTCONF configuration plane using /restconf/*, while sharing the same TLS and authentication infrastructure.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 [RFC2119] [RFC8174] when, and only when, they appear in all capitals.

A non-agent upper-layer system or user-facing application that uses the A2U interface. Examples include an operator's OSS/BSS systems, orchestrators, management portals, automation systems, and human-facing applications. An upper-layer NMA is not an A2U Client in this document.
A goal description submitted to the NMA. It can be expressed using natural language or structured data.

An Agent-to-Agent interface used for interaction between agents or NMAs. A2A is outside the scope of this document.

The Agent-to-Network interface between the NMA and network resources, or the corresponding extended southbound capability in an integrated deployment.

section.name: Scope
section.t: This document defines:

ul.li: a single YANG data model for A2U objects;
a non-normative HTTP-based protocol binding example.

section.t: This document does not define:

ul.li: domain-specific service models, such as optical network service models or IP network service models;
detailed A2C or A2N protocol mechanisms;

section.name: A2U Interface Positioning
section.t: A2U is used when a non-agent upper-layer system or user invokes NMA capabilities.
In the A2U model:

ul.li: the A2U Client is a non-agent system or user;
the client submits intents or requests;
the NMA manages parsing, planning, execution, confirmation, event reporting, and result generation;
the client observes, confirms, or aborts the task when required.

section.t: A2U is not used when an upper-layer NMA communicates with a lower-layer NMA. Such communication is Agent-to-Agent communication and should use A2A or other Agent-to-Agent interfaces, because both sides may need peer-agent semantics such as capability negotiation, task delegation, collaboration, commitment, trust establishment, and result aggregation.
The A2U interface is distinct from:

ul.li: A2A, used between agents or NMAs;
A2C, used between the NMA and controller functions;
A2N, used between the NMA and network resources.

section.name: A2U Reference Framework
section.t: The figure below follows the integrated deployment mode of the NMA architecture. In this mode, the NMA is integrated with the Network Controller as part of an enhanced controller platform. The controller functions are shown on the left and the NMA functions are shown on the right.

section.t: The A2U Service Function provides capability discovery, intent submission, task monitoring, plan exposure, confirmation handling, event notification, and result reporting.

The A2U data model defined in this document focuses only on information exchanged across A2U. It does not define the internal NMA architecture, internal A2C mechanisms, or extended southbound mechanisms.

In the independent deployment mode, the NMA may be deployed beside the Network Controller. In that case, the NMA exposes A2U upward, interacts with the controller through A2C, and interacts with network resources through A2N.

section.name: Logical Separation
section.t: In an HTTP-based realization, A2U may share the controller's HTTPS port, TLS session, and authentication system, but it is logically separated from the configuration plane.
For example:

ul.li: /restconf/* may be used for RESTCONF configuration and operational datastore access;
/nma/a2u/* may be used for A2U interaction.

section.name: Protocol-Binding Independence
section.t: The A2U YANG model defines information objects and message structures. It does not mandate HTTP, RESTCONF, NETCONF, gRPC, or any other protocol binding.

section.name: Unified Intent Entry
section.t: Natural-language and structured input share the same intent submission entry and the same task lifecycle. The mode field distinguishes the input type.

section.name: Unified Task Lifecycle
section.t: After an intent is accepted, the NMA creates or associates a task. The task lifecycle includes:

figure.name: Lifecycle of a task
figure.artwork: PENDING -> ANALYZING -> PLANNING -> AWAITING_CONFIRMATION -> EXECUTING -> COMPLETED / FAILED / ABORTED

section.t: Clarification may be requested when input is incomplete or ambiguous.

section.name: Human-in-the-Loop Confirmation
section.t: When a task exceeds an autonomy level, violates a policy, affects critical resources, or requires human review, the NMA creates a confirmation object and suspends execution until the confirmation is resolved.

section.name: Event Streaming and Polling
section.t: The NMA reports task progress through typed events. Events may be delivered by streaming, polling, or other binding-specific mechanisms.

section.name: A2U Information Model
section.t: The A2U information model contains five core components.

section.name: Agent Capabilities
section.t: The agent-capabilities object, also called the Agent Card, describes the NMA and its exposed skills. It includes:

ul.li: optional tags for skill classification and discovery;

section.name: Intent
section.t: The intent object represents a user or system goal. It includes:
Natural-language input may include the original user text, parsed result, and parser type. Structured input includes operation type, target resource, constraints, and priority.

The intent-type identifies the high-level operation category. It is not intended to encode all domain-specific subtypes. Domain-specific details, such as service assurance objectives, fault symptoms, recovery constraints, or optimization policies, are carried in the constraints field.

The base operation categories include creation, deletion, modification, query, reporting, diagnosis, remediation, optimization, and assurance. For example, service assurance is represented by ASSURE; fault analysis is represented by DIAGNOSE; corrective fault handling or service recovery is represented by REMEDIATE.

section.name: Task
section.t: The task object represents the lifecycle of an accepted intent. It includes:
The plan is a list of steps. The audit log records important task actions.

section.name: Confirmation
section.t: The confirmation object represents a pending or resolved decision point. It includes:
The resolution container records the final decision made for a confirmation, including the selected action, any modified parameters, the resolver, and the resolution time.

section.name: Event
section.t: The event object represents task-related notifications. It includes:
The event payload is modeled as a choice so that different event types carry different payload structures.

section.name: Model Design
section.t: This document defines a single YANG module, ietf-nma-a2u.

The module uses the YANG data structure extension defined in [RFC8791]. The sx:structure statements describe abstract information objects and message bodies exchanged across A2U. They are not configuration datastore nodes.

Only the top-level structures use the nma-a2u- prefix in their names, in order to distinguish A2U structures from other future NMA interface structures. Fields inside the structures keep short names for readability.
The reusable groupings use the -object suffix, such as intent-object and task-object, to distinguish reusable object templates from instantiated containers and top-level structures.

section.name: YANG Module
Security Considerations
section.t: The A2U interface can expose sensitive operational information, including intents, tasks, plans, affected resources, confirmation context, event streams, and audit information.
Implementations are expected to provide authentication, authorization, confidentiality protection, integrity protection, replay protection, audit logging, and policy enforcement.

Natural-language inputs and AI-assisted interpretation may introduce risks such as ambiguous instructions, malicious input, prompt injection, or incorrect interpretation. Implementations should validate interpreted results before execution and should use confirmation or policy checks for risky operations.
Confirmation resolution operations can affect network behavior and therefore require authorization and audit logging.
Event streams may contain sensitive operational information. Implementations should ensure that event subscribers are authorized to receive the corresponding events.
Future versions of this document are expected to expand this section.

section.name: Example HTTP-Based Binding
section.t: This appendix describes one possible HTTP-based realization of the A2U interface. It is provided as an example protocol binding and is not intended to mandate HTTP as the only implementation mechanism.

section.name: General Rules
section.t: In this example binding:

ul.li: A2U resources use the /nma/a2u/* URI space;
RESTCONF resources may use the /restconf/* URI space;
JSON is used for request and response bodies;
Server-Sent Events (SSE) may be used for event streaming;
TLS, authentication, authorization, and audit logging are required by the implementation.

section.name: Capability Discovery
section.t: Response body: nma-a2u-agent-capabilities.

section.name: Intent Submission
section.t: Request body: nma-a2u-submit-intent-request.
Response body: nma-a2u-submit-intent-response.
Possible responses include:

ul.li: 200 OK with text/event-stream for streaming scenarios.

section.name: Task Retrieval
section.t: Response body: nma-a2u-task.

section.name: Task Listing

section.name: JSON Examples
section.t: This appendix provides non-normative JSON examples for an OTN fault handling and service assurance scenario.

In this example, an OSS detects degradation of an OTN service and invokes the NMA through A2U. The NMA analyzes alarms and performance data, correlates service impact, identifies the likely root cause, generates a recovery plan, requests confirmation, and reports task progress through events.
